textbookText: Truncus arteriosus is further divisible into a proximal or basal muscular part called conus arteriosus and the distal thinwalled bulbous aretriosus. The inner hollow cavities inside the conus arteriosus and bulbous arteriosus are called pylangium and synangium respectively. A row of the three semilunar valves separates the pylangium from the synangium.The pylangium is further divided incompletely into two chambers by a vertical and spirally twisted valve called spiral valve. The right chamber is the cavum aorticum and the left chamber is called the cavum pulmocutaneum. The spiral valve is attached dorsally but its ventral edge is free. In the cavum pulmocutaneum lies a common opening of pulmocutaneous arches. This opening is also guarded by a valve. The synangium bifurcates into two branches as right aortic trunk and and left aortic trunk. Each aortic trunk divides into three arches, the pulmocutaneous, systemic and carotid arches.

3. Working of Heart: Heart of frog is myogenic (heart beat originates from the heart muscles itself). Rhythmic contraction and relaxation of the heart is called heartbeat. Heart continuously beats during the life span which is under the nervous control to pump blood throughout the body. Contraction phase of ventricle is called systole and relaxation phase is called diastole. Wave of contraction originates from the sinus venosus and spreads over its wall and auricles. The sinus venosus contracts, whose contraction drives the mixed blood from the sinus venosus to the right auricle. The backward flow of the blood from right auricle to the sinus venosus is checked by the sinuauricular valves. Meanwhile, the left auricle also receives oxygenated blood through pulmonary veins from the lungs. When the two auricles are full of blood, they contract simultaneously. The blood cannot go back into pulmonary veins as the openings of the pulmonary veins are small and oblique which are closed automatically by the contraction of the left auricle. Thus, blood from both auricles is pumped into the single ventricle through auriculoventricular aperture. Now, wave of the contraction is passed over the wall of the ventricle. There are two views regarding how the ventricle pumps blood through the truncus arteriosus:

a. Old view or conventional view According to this view given by Brucke 1858, the ventricle contains impure blood in the right side received from the right auricle, mixed blood in middle region and pure or oxygenated blood in the left side from the left auricle. Whole Blood can’t get mixed thoroughly because of viscosity of blood and presence of columnae carnea on the inner wall of ventricle. When the ventricle contracts, deoxygenated blood from its right side passes into cavum pulmocutaneum and is then carried to the lungs and skin for oxygenation. The spiral valve doesnot allow the blood to pass into the cavum aorticum at this time. Then, opening of cavum pulmocutaneum is closed by spiral valve. Next, mixed blood is pumped into cavum aorticum which passes through

systemic arches. Finally, oxygenated blood from the left side is passed through cavum aorticum into the carotid arches which flow to the head region. Thus, spiral valve in truncus arteriosus play major role in directing blood in different arches. b. Modern View According to the modern view, both oxygenated and deoxygenated blood s are mixed in the ventricle. When the ventricle contracts and the backward flow of blood into auricles are prevented by the auriculo-ventricular valve, the mixed blood of the ventricle enters the truncus arteriosus. From the truncus arteriosus mixed blood goes to three arches (carotid, systemic and pulmocutaneous) and reaches all the parts of the body.

By this view, It is concluded that there is complete mixing of blood in ventricle, spiral valve is nonfunctional and blood leaving from truncus arteriosus is mixed blood which circulates throughout the body. B. BLOOD VESSELS Blood vessels are tubes or channels of variable sizes forming the complex network in the body of frog. Their prime function is to transport blood among the various parts of the body. There is unidirectional flow of blood in blood vessels. Blood vessels are of three types 1. Arteries: They are muscular, elastic and thick-walled blood vessels. Arteries transport blood from heart to the various parts of the body. They have narrow lumen. There is more pressure of blood in arteries and hence they are without valves. To withstand such a great pressure, they have thick wall. They are deeply seated in the body and transport oxygenated blood but in frog, arteries transport mixed blood. These blood vessels do not collapse easily after death because of their thicker and rigid wall. Arteries divide into smaller branches called arterioles and arterioles divide into capillaries.
